QF.id: AIFM Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_1

question.text: Mr. Ramesh Iyer, a junior investment analyst at Saraswati Capital AIF, is studying the foundations of portfolio construction used by the fund's quantitative team. His senior asks him who formally quantified the benefits of diversification using the statistical notion of covariance, giving birth to what is today known as Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT). Which of the following statements is MOST accurate?

answer.text: Eugene Fama, in the 1970s, first demonstrated portfolio variance using a multi-factor framework and is considered the father of MPT.
William Sharpe in 1964, through the development of the Capital Asset Pricing Model, published the paper that introduced Modern Portfolio Theory.

Harry Markowitz, in his 1952 Journal of Finance paper titled 'Portfolio Selection', mathematically demonstrated that the variance of returns is a meaningful measure of portfolio risk; he received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990.
Stephen Ross developed MPT in 1976 as an extension of the Arbitrage Pricing Theory.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 4 explicitly states that MPT was introduced by Harry Markowitz in a 1952 Journal of Finance article titled 'Portfolio Selection'. He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1990. He introduced covariance/correlation to quantify diversification benefit and derived portfolio variance as a risk measure. The Trap: Sharpe (1964), Lintner, Mossin, and Treynor developed CAPM in the 1960s — that is Capital Market Theory, not MPT. Fama is associated with Efficient Market Hypothesis and the Fama-French factors. Ross developed APT (1976), not MPT. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A/B Distributor exams and XXI-B (Portfolio Managers) also carry this same attribution question. Research Analyst (XV) and Investment Adviser L1/L2 (X-A/X-B) expect candidates to cite the 1952 Markowitz paper correctly. Manager's Pro-Tip: When briefing the IC on why you propose a correlation-diversified AIF fund-of-funds, always anchor the framework on Markowitz (1952). LPs with CIO-level oversight expect GPs to demonstrate theoretical literacy, not just private-market intuition.
